planting.note: Plant in consistently moist, silty clay soil in part sun; this federally endangered species spreads by rhizomes to form dense colonial patches rather than climbing far, so no trellis is required.

directions: A federally endangered species known from only a handful of sites in Alabama and Georgia, the Alabama leather flower spreads underground by rhizomes into dense clonal patches in seepy, silty-clay openings among sedges rather than scrambling widely like most clematis. In spring it produces small, nodding, urn-shaped flowers typical of the leatherflower (Viorna) group, with thick, leathery purple-tinged sepals that barely open. Because its wild habitat stays consistently damp, cultivated plants need steady moisture and should never be allowed to dry out, and given its rarity any garden stock should come only from nursery-propagated material.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Plant in sharply drained, calcareous or shaly soil in sun to light shade; this shale-barren endemic resents heavy wet soils and needs excellent drainage to persist.

directions: Endemic to a small cluster of counties in western Virginia, the Virginia whitehair leather flower grows on dry shale barrens and calcareous rock woodlands, a habitat that demands lean, fast-draining soil and full exposure to be grown successfully in a garden. Like other members of the leatherflower (Viorna) group it produces small, nodding, thick-sepaled urn-shaped flowers rather than the broad open blooms of large-flowered hybrids, with a weak-climbing, scrambling habit low to the ground. Its name reflects the dense, whitish, felt-like hairs covering its foliage, a distinguishing feature from related leatherflower species. Site it where winter wet is minimal and avoid rich garden soil, which encourages rot rather than growth.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

common_name: Tango Clematis (Mauve-Purple Viticella Clematis Edged in Cream)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Tango is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Bred in Poland as part of a group of viticella cultivars given dance names, Tango bears medium-sized, nodding flowers in mauve-purple with each tepal margined in contrasting creamy white. Like other viticella types it flowers prolifically on the current season's growth from midsummer into early fall, so the whole vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3). Its strongly bicolor edging sets it apart from solid-colored viticella cultivars and makes it a striking companion for scrambling through a spent early shrub rose.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; this non-vining botanical variety forms a woody-based mound and needs no climbing support.

directions: This Chinese botanical variety of the sub-shrubby C. heracleifolia is grown chiefly for its strongly fragrant, tubular, deep blue flowers with frilled, recurved sepal tips, carried in dense clusters at the leaf axils from late summer into fall. Rather than climbing, it forms a coarse-leaved, non-vining mound that works well massed at the front of a sunny border alongside other late-season herbaceous perennials. It is the wild variety behind several named garden selections but differs from them in being an unselected, straight botanical form raised from wild-collected stock. Cut the woody-based stems back hard in late winter to keep growth dense and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant in rocky, well-drained, often calcareous soil in part shade; this cold-hardy North American Atragene-group species climbs modestly by twining leaf stalks on rock ledges or low shrubs.

directions: Native to rocky, calcareous woodlands, ledges, and talus slopes from Quebec and the Canadian Rockies south to the northern Appalachians and upper Midwest, purple virgin's bower is one of only a few North American members of the Atragene group that also includes the Eurasian C. alpina and C. macropetala. In spring it produces nodding, bell-shaped, blue-purple flowers with four broad sepals, opening before most other native vines and followed by attractive plumed seed heads. It climbs only modestly by twining petioles rather than true tendrils, making it suitable for scrambling over a low rock wall or through a small shrub rather than covering a large structure. Exceptionally cold-hardy, it is a good choice for a native-plant rock garden in climates too harsh for most garden clematis hybrids.

planting.note: Plant with roots shaded and top growth in sun; this California chaparral native is drought-tolerant once established and needs minimal summer water.

directions: Native to dry foothills, canyons, and streamside woodlands of California and Baja California, chaparral clematis is a robust, woody climber that produces masses of small, creamy-white, star-shaped flowers with yellow stamens from early spring into early summer. After bloom it remains ornamental thanks to silky, plumed seed heads that persist into winter. Like most clematis it prefers its roots kept cool and shaded while the top growth reaches into full sun, and it is well suited to climbing into an oak, toyon, or other native shrub in a low-water, chaparral-style planting. Once established it is markedly drought tolerant and needs little supplemental irrigation.

planting.note: Plant along a fence row or let it scramble into shrubs in full sun; this Southwestern native tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with minimal care.

directions: Native to Texas, Arizona, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, old man's beard is a vigorous, semi-woody vine that scrambles over fences and shrubs across prairies and desert grasslands. Its small flowers are inconspicuous, but because the species is dioecious, female plants follow bloom with a spectacular show of fruits trailing silvery, three-inch plumed tails from late summer into fall, giving the species its common name. It tolerates both extended drought and occasional moisture, performing best in well-drained soil in full sun with little supplemental care once established. Its toughness and showy seed heads make it a valuable, low-maintenance native for a Southwestern or xeric wildlife garden.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy support; flowers on new growth, so cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Native to southern Europe and North Africa, fragrant virgin's bower is a vigorous deciduous climber smothered in late summer and autumn with masses of small, star-shaped white flowers carrying an intense sweet almond scent, especially noticeable after rain or in the evening. Glossy dark green foliage sets off the flowers well, and blooms give way to the fluffy, silvery seed heads typical of the species group. Because it flowers entirely on the current season's growth, the whole vine can be cut back hard to near ground level each late winter (Group 3) without sacrificing bloom. Give it a sturdy fence, large shrub, or tree to scramble into, since it can cover significant ground in a single season once established.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy support; flowers on new growth, so cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Native to a broad swath of central and eastern Asia, oriental clematis is a vigorous scrambling species named for the thick, waxy texture of its nodding yellow flowers, whose four broad, recurved sepals have a faintly citrusy appearance recalling orange peel. Flowers appear from midsummer through late autumn, each with a prominent cluster of red-tipped stamens, followed by the fluffy silvery seed heads typical of the later-blooming clematis species. It flowers only on the current season's growth, so it can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3) to keep its rampant growth in check. Give it a sturdy fence or large shrub to scramble through, and be aware it can self-seed and naturalize readily in favorable climates.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade with a sturdy support; flowers on new growth, so cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Native to the Korean Peninsula, Manchuria, and the Russian Far East, Korean clematis is closely related to the better-known golden-flowered tangutica group but bears smaller, pale yellow, nodding bell-shaped flowers with a distinct lemon scent and dark purple anthers. Bloom runs from late summer into fall over about a month, followed by the silky silvery seedheads typical of its relatives, adding interest into winter. It tolerates both calcareous and acidic soils and flowers entirely on the current season's growth, so the whole vine can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3). Its citrus fragrance and smaller, more refined flower size distinguish it from larger-flowered tangutica cultivars.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy support; flowers on new growth, so cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Native to China and Japan, October clematis is a free-flowering deciduous climber related to the more rampant C. vitalba but notably less vigorous and easier to contain in a garden setting. From late summer into early fall it produces masses of small, slightly fragrant, dull white star-shaped flowers held above deeply toothed, celery-like leaflets, the resemblance giving rise to its species name. Like other late-blooming species it flowers on the current season's growth, so the whole vine can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3) without losing bloom. It needs a sunny position to flower well and makes a good, moderately sized alternative to larger late-season species for covering a fence or arbor.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy support; flowers over a long season on new growth, so cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Native to western China, this vigorous scrambling species bears satiny, pure white flowers with prominent yellow stamens, produced singly or a few together at the leaf axils over an unusually long season from early summer into fall. It is the straight wild species behind garden hybrids bred for extended bloom, such as the trade-named Summer Snow, but differs from those named hybrids in its smaller, more refined flower form and unselected habit. Being a long, rampant grower, it needs a sturdy fence, large shrub, or tree to climb into, and flowering occurs entirely on new growth, so the whole vine can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3) to control size.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, evenly moist soil in a bright spot shielded from harsh drying sun; a non-vining clematis that needs no climbing support.

directions: A white-flowered selection of the herbaceous bush clematis, Alba produces dainty, nodding, bell-shaped flowers of pure white, sometimes with a faint blush of blue at the base of the tepals, from early to midsummer above a clump of simple, un-lobed leaves. Like other integrifolia types it forms a lax, self-supporting, non-climbing mound rather than a true vine, making it useful for weaving through the front of a border or draping over a low wall. Flowers give way to attractive silvery seed heads that extend interest into early fall. Cut the whole plant back close to the ground in late winter, since bloom forms entirely on new growth each year.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
